Date: 2026-07-15
Time: 10:00 PDT / 17:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Marco Nguyen (Redwood SE), Sara Gomez (Helix Head of ML), Ethan Park (Helix Lead DS), Ravi Menon (Helix Security), Maya Lin (Helix PM)
summary: Weekly POC sync to review quality evaluation, regression checks, and guardrail tuning for Helix Diagnostics pilot. Discussed scoring thresholds, prompt set regressions, edge-case failures, security requirements for VPC/KMS, and next steps for benching latency/cost on a dedicated run.
topics: quality evaluation; regression checks; prompt set A/B; scoring thresholds; guardrails/false positives; security (SOC2, KMS, VPC); dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs; benchmark plan
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then we'll jump to the scoring updates.
[00:12] Sara Gomez: Hi, Sara here. Good morning.
[00:15] Ethan Park: Ethan, hi.
[00:17] Ravi Menon: Ravi on security.
[00:19] Maya Lin: Maya here.
[00:22] Priya Patel: Priya from Redwood, hi all.
[00:25] Marco Nguyen: Marco as well.
[00:28] Jordan Lee: Great. Last week we flagged the regression in the diagnosis-normalization prompt set where precision fell about 6 points vs baseline. Priya, do you want to walk through what we changed?
[00:40] Priya Patel: Yeah, sure. So we ran the automated eval against the 2k prompt subset, and the main drift appears tied to a prompt mutation that introduced more conversational context; the model started hallucinating extra qualifiers, like 'likely' vs the ground truth numeric code. We tried adjusting the stop sequences and tightened the post-filtering scorer; that recovered about half the drop but there are still edge cases.
[01:05] Ethan Park: Do you have examples of the hallucinations? That 'likely' vs exact code is pretty bad for downstream billing mapping.
[01:12] Priya Patel: Yep. Example 1: input 'patient reports intermittent chest pain' expected CPT code 93000, model returned '93000, likely 93005' — that's the extra qualifier. Example 2: small snippet where the model appended a sentence, which broke our parser.
[01:30] Sara Gomez: Right, so for Helix we need deterministic outputs for the mapping step. We can tolerate a softer phrasing in summaries, but the code mappings must be exact.
[01:40] Jordan Lee: Understood. That's where the guardrails and stricter scoring thresholds come in. Marco, show the scoring spreadsheet?
[01:47] Marco Nguyen: Sharing now (link: drive.redwood/helix/poc/scoring-v2). So current scoring: exact match weight 0.7, token-similarity 0.2, penalty for extra tokens 0.1. We proposed bumping exact-match to 0.85 and increasing penalty for extraneous tokens.
[02:10] Ethan Park: If we bump exact-match that hard will we increase false negatives? I'm worried about valid variants being rejected.
[02:18] Priya Patel: Good point. That's why our recommendation is to run A/B on the Helix corpus: keep current weighting vs strict weighting and measure recall/precision tradeoffs. We ran a small pilot — strict weighting raised precision to 0.93 but recall dropped from 0.88 to 0.81 on ambiguous phrasings.
[02:38] Maya Lin: Ambiguous phrasings are common in our triage notes. Can we add a fallback path? Like if exact-match fails but token-similarity passes above 0.92, then we route to a human-in-the-loop or a secondary rule engine.
[02:50] Priya Patel: Yes, that's a pattern we recommend: soft-fail -> escalate. Redwood also supports prefix caching so common exact mappings are ultra-fast and can be prioritized.
[03:02] Ravi Menon: On the security side, if we escalate to humans, what audit logs do we get? We need immutable logs for compliance.
[03:09] Jordan Lee: We capture request-level logs with redaction policies; for Private/VPC deployments you can retain full audit trails in your S3/KMS bucket, and Redwood can provide HMAC traces. We'll send the SOC2/network diagram section you requested.
[03:25] Ravi Menon: Need to confirm KMS flow — we can't have plaintext keys on vendor side.
[03:29] Priya Patel: For VPC Private, we support customer-managed KMS where the customer holds CMKs; Redwood integrates with common cloud KMS (AWS KMS, GCP CMEK). We can document the envelope encryption flow.
[03:42] Ethan Park: Back to quality, we saw a regression specifically on the 'medication interaction' prompt set after we increased max tokens for one variant. Could the longer context be causing the KV cache to evict relevant tokens?
[03:53] Marco Nguyen: Possibly; longer sequences change attention patterns and the runtime will pick different kernels. But on hosted runs we saw only a small latency bump. For Dedicated, you can pin quantization and kernel selection to stabilize behavior.
[04:08] Sara Gomez: We're trying to decide hosted vs dedicated. Latency matters during peak throughput but budgets are tight. Can you remind us of the cost/latency tradeoffs?
[04:16] Jordan Lee: Sure. Hosted gives fast onboarding and lower ops; Dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower unit cost at scale. Our Optimize tool suggested a quantization profile that reduces token cost by ~25% with a ~5% quality delta on your test corpus. We can run a dedicated benchmark that simulates your 2k concurrent user workload.
[04:36] Maya Lin: That benchmark would help procurement. Please include tail latency P95/P99.
[04:41] Priya Patel: Will do. We'll include P50/P95/P99 and cost per 1k tokens with and without caching.
[04:48] Ethan Park: On guardrails — we need to reduce false positives where the guardrail incorrectly flags valid outputs. What tuning knobs are available?
[04:55] Priya Patel: Two levers: stricter pattern-matching on post-filters and a learned classifier for safety that runs as a secondary check. The classifier can be tuned to be conservative or permissive. We propose running a calibration run: collect 5k outputs, label them quickly, and train the classifier to your tolerance curve.
[05:13] Sara Gomez: How long to get that calibration done?
[05:16] Priya Patel: With your team labeling at 100 labels/hour, 5k labels is ~50 hours; Redwood can assist with accelerated labeling for an additional engagement. Alternatively, start with the rule-based approach for faster iteration.
[05:30] Ethan Park: For the A/B prompt-variation tests, are we using the same temperature and sampling settings?
[05:34] Marco Nguyen: Yes, we kept sampling consistent. The changes were exclusively in prompt phrasing and max tokens. We'll provide the exact run config in the spreadsheet.
[05:44] Maya Lin: Can we also capture the parser failure rate? A lot of downstream issues are parser exceptions when the model returns extra sentences.
[05:50] Priya Patel: We'll add parser-exception as a metric in the spreadsheet. Current parser failure rate is 2.3% on the latest run. The extra tokens correlate strongly with parser failures.
[06:02] Jordan Lee: Ok let's recap action items. Jordan will send the scoring spreadsheet update; Priya will run guardrail tuning and propose two configs; Ethan will run A/B tests and upload results; Ravi will look at SOC2/KMS notes. We'll also schedule the dedicated benchmark.
[06:18] Sara Gomez: Sounds good. One quick question — any showstopper regressions that would pause the POC?
[06:23] Priya Patel: Nothing that can't be mitigated. The regressions are operational (parser fragility, false positives) rather than model-architecture issues. With guardrails + stricter scoring we can keep the POC moving.
[06:35] Ethan Park: Agree. We'll proceed with the A/B and the fallback path.
[06:40] Jordan Lee: Great. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and updated spreadsheet. Meeting adjourned.
[06:46] Maya Lin: Thanks.
[06:48] Ravi Menon: Thanks all.
[06:50] Marco Nguyen: Thanks.
